Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 48, verse 1:

Surat al-Fath is Medinan, and it was revealed concerning the return of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from al-Hudaybiyya. Its verses number twenty-nine.

﴿Indeed, We have granted you a clear conquest﴾. Fath al-balad (the conquest of a land) is an expression for gaining victory over it, whether by force (ʿanwatan) or by agreement (ṣulḥan), with fighting or without it. For what has not been taken is "mughlaq" (closed), and the word is derived from opening the door of a house (fatḥ bab al-dar). Its attribution to the plural of majesty (nūn al-ʿaẓama) is because the actions of the servants are ascribed to Allah, the Exalted, in terms of creation and bringing into being. The intended meaning is the conquest of Makkah, may Allah ennoble it, which is narrated from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was given glad tidings of it when he was returning from al-Hudaybiyya. The expression of it in the past tense, according to the pattern of all the divine reports, serves to announce that it will certainly come to pass, as an emphasis on the glad tidings, just as opening the statement with the particle of certainty (ḥarf al-taḥqīq) is for this purpose. In it there is a majesty that indicates the greatness of the status of the One who informs, glory be to Him and mighty is His authority, which is not hidden. It has been said: it is what was made available to him, upon him be prayer and peace, in that year of the conquest of Khaybar, and this is narrated from Mujahid. It has been said: it is the treaty of al-Hudaybiyya, for although there was no fierce fighting in it, but rather shooting between the two groups with arrows and stones, yet since the ascendancy belonged to the Muslims when the polytheists asked them for a truce, it was undoubtedly a conquest. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) that they shot at the polytheists until they drove them into their homes. And from al-Kalbi: they prevailed over them until they asked for a truce. It has indeed been narrated that when it reached him, upon him be prayer and peace, that a man said: "This is not a conquest; we have been barred from the House and our offering has been barred," he said: "Rather, it is the greatest of conquests. The polytheists have agreed to repel you by means of the peace, and have asked you for a settlement, and have sought safety from you, and they have seen from you what they dislike." And from al-Shaʿbi: it was revealed at al-Hudaybiyya, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) obtained in that expedition what he had not obtained in any other expedition, for he was given the pledge of al-Ridwan, and his past and future sins were forgiven, and the offering reached its place, and they were fed the dates of Khaybar, and the Romans prevailed over the Persians, so the Muslims rejoiced at it. And there was in the conquest of al-Hudaybiyya a great sign, namely that its water was drawn out until no drop remained in it, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rinsed his mouth and then spat it into the well, and it gushed with water until everyone who was with him drank and was satisfied. It has been said: the water surged until it was full and its water did not run out afterwards. It has been said: it is the whole of the conquests that Allah opened for him, upon him be prayer and peace, of Islam, prophethood and the call, by proof and by the sword, and there is no conquest more manifest or greater than it, and it is the head of all conquests, since no conquest of Islam occurs except that it is a branch of its branches and a offshoot of its offshoots. It has been said: al-fath here means judgement (al-qaḍāʾ), and from it comes "infitāḥuhu lil-ḥukūma" (his opening up to arbitration), and the meaning is: We have decided for you against the people of Makkah that you will enter it in the following year, and this is narrated from Qatadah (may Allah be pleased with him). Whatever the case, the omission of the object is for the purpose of focusing on the act itself and to indicate that the ground of the glad tidings is the very conquest proceeding from Him, glory be to Him, and not the particularity of the thing conquered.

﴿a manifest conquest﴾: clear, evident in its matter and plain in its circumstances, or distinguishing between truth and falsehood.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 48, verse 2:**

And His saying, ﴿That Allah may forgive you﴾, is a purpose (ghayah) of the conquest (al-fath), inasmuch as it is consequent upon his striving, upon him be blessings and peace, in raising high the word of Allah, the Exalted, by enduring the hardships of wars and plunging into the sources of calamities. And the turning (iltifat) to the Name of the Essence (ism al-dhat), which entails all the attributes, serves to indicate that each of the actions strung together in the thread of this purpose proceeds from Him, the Exalted, from an aspect different from the aspect of the other, and is consequent upon one of His attributes, the Exalted.

﴿Whatever of your sin has been past and whatever is to come﴾: that is, all that has transpired from you of leaving the better course (tark al-awla). Calling it a sin is in view of his exalted station.

﴿And complete His favor upon you﴾ by raising high the religion and joining sovereignty to prophethood, and other of the blessings, religious and worldly, that He bestowed upon him.

﴿And guide you to a straight path﴾ in conveying the message and establishing the ceremonies of leadership. The root of uprightness, although it was already attained before the conquest, there was obtained after it, from the clarifying of the paths of truth and the uprightness of its methods, what had not been obtained before.

Translation:

﴿And Allah will help you﴾: The explicit mention of the Majestic Name (Allah) is for the reason that it comes as the culmination of the aims (of the verse), and in order to show the full extent of concern for the matter of victory, as is indicated by its emphasis through His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a mighty victory﴾, i.e., a victory in which there is might and invulnerability, or a strong, unassailable victory, with the attribute of the noun (the victory) being given the attribute of its possessor (the one who achieves it) metaphorically, for the sake of emphasis; or (it means) a victory whose possessor is mighty.

[Qur'an 48:4] "It is He who sent down tranquility (al-sakinah) into the hearts of the believers..."

Tranquility (al-sakinah) is an explanation of what He bestowed upon them of the beginnings of victory: firmness and calm, i.e., He sent it down.

"...into the hearts of the believers" — because of the reconciliation and security, to manifest His grace upon them by facilitating security after fear.

"...that they might increase in faith along with their faith" — i.e., certainty added to their certainty. Or: He sent down into them tranquility toward what the Prophet (peace be upon him) brought of the laws, so that they might increase in faith in them, coupled with their faith in the Oneness (of God) and the Last Day. From Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father): the first thing the Prophet (ﷺ) brought them was monotheism (tawhid), then prayer and zakat, then hajj and jihad, and so they increased in faith along with their faith. Or: He sent down into them dignity and reverence for Allah the Exalted and His Messenger, so that by believing in this they might increase in faith beyond their faith.

"And to Allah belong the hosts of the heavens and the earth" — He manages their affairs as He wills: He empowers some of them over others at times, and at other times brings peace between them, as His will requires, which is founded upon wisdoms and interests.

"And Allah is ever Knowing" — exceedingly so in knowledge of all matters.

"Wise" — in His decree and His management.

Translation:

"That He may admit the believing men and believing women into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever" is connected to what is implied by the mention that the hosts of the heavens and the earth belong to Him, Exalted is He, in the sense of management and disposal. That is: He ordained what He ordained of empowering the believers, so that they would recognize God's favor in that and give thanks for it, and so that He would admit them to Paradise.

"And He will remove from them their misdeeds" means He covers them and does not expose them. The mention of admission before removal of misdeeds, although the order in existence is the reverse, is to hasten to the statement of what is the highest aim.

"And that is" means: what was mentioned of admission and removal of misdeeds.

"With God it is a great triumph" whose measure cannot be estimated, because it is the furthest point that the necks of aspirations stretch toward, in terms of bringing benefit and repelling harm. "With God" is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) qualifying "triumph," because it was originally its attribute; when it was placed before it, it became a circumstantial phrase, meaning: being with God, that is, in His knowledge and His decree. The clause is a parenthetical insertion (i'tirāḍ) that confirms what precedes it.

﴿And He punishes the hypocrite men and the hypocrite women, and the polytheist men and the polytheist women﴾ is coordinated with "He admits." Placing the hypocrites before the polytheists clearly indicates that they deserve the punishment more than the polytheists do.

﴿Who think ill of God, an ill thought﴾: that is, they think an evil thing about the matter, namely that He will not give victory to His Messenger and the believers. ﴿Upon them is a circle of evil﴾: that is, what they imagine and wait for against the believers will encompass them and turn back upon them. It is also read "dā'iratu al-sū'" (with a ḍammah on the sīn). The two are dialects derived from sā'a (to be evil), like al-kurh and al-karh (both meaning "dislike"). The only difference is that the fatḥah form (dā'iratu al-saw') became the usual form for attaching whatever is to be condemned from any thing, while the ḍammah form (dā'iratu al-sū') functions as the equivalent of "evil."

﴿And God became wrathful toward them, and cursed them, and prepared for them Jahannam﴾: this is coordinated with what they deserve in the Hereafter, based on what they earned in this world. The wāw (the conjunction "and") is used in the last two clauses, although the proper particle would be the fā' (the conjunction "so/then"), which indicates that what precedes it is the cause of what follows. The wāw is used to signal that each of the two is independent in the threat and original in its own right, without treating one as a consequence of the other.

﴿And evil is it as a destination﴾: that is, Jahannam.

(p-106) ﴿And to Allah belong the hosts of the heavens and the earth; and Allah is ever Mighty, Wise.﴾ This is a repetition of what preceded. They said: its benefit is to alert that Allah, exalted, has hosts of mercy and hosts of punishment, and that what is intended here is the hosts of punishment, as is indicated by the mention of the attribute of might (ʿizza).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 48, verse 8:

﴿Indeed, We have sent you as a witness﴾ i.e., over your ummah (community), in accordance with His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿and the Messenger will be a witness over you﴾.

﴿and a bringer of good tidings﴾ of obedience.

﴿and a warner﴾ against disobedience.

﴿That you may believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ) and to his community.

﴿And support him﴾, that is, strengthen him by strengthening his religion and his Messenger.

﴿And honour him﴾, that is, magnify him.

﴿And glorify Him﴾, that is, declare Him far above imperfection, or pray to Him, from the word *al-subḥah* (voluntary prayer).

﴿Morning and evening﴾, that is, at dawn and at dusk. From Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him): the prayer of Fajr, the prayer of Zuhr, and the prayer of 'Asr. The four verbs are also read with the initial letter in the third person, *yā'* (with a dot below), as *yu'minū*, *yu'azzirūhu*, *yuwaqqirūhu*, and *yusabbiḥūhu*. The reading *wa-tu'zirūhu* is recited with a *ḍammah* on the *tā'* and a light *zā'* with a *kasrah*. Another reading is with a *fatḥah* on the *tā'* and a *ḍammah* or *kasrah* on the *zā'*, *wa-tu'azzizūhu*, with two *zā'*s. And *wa-tuwqirūhu* is from *awqara*, which has the same meaning as *waqqara* (to honour).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 48, verse 10:

﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you﴾ means: to fight the Quraysh, under the tree. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿they pledge allegiance only to Allah﴾ is a predicate (khabar), meaning: your pledge of allegiance is the pledge of allegiance to Allah, mighty and majestic, because the intent is to confirm the covenant by observing His commands and prohibitions. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿the hand of Allah is over their hands﴾ is either a circumstantial clause (hal) or a resumptive clause (isti'naf) emphasizing it, in the manner of imagery (takhyil). The meaning is that the contracting of the covenant with the Messenger is like contracting it with Allah, exalted is He, without any difference between the two, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah﴾. It was also read as "innama yubayi'una Allah" (they pledge allegiance only for Allah), meaning: for His sake and for His countenance.

﴿So whoever breaks [his oath], it is only to his own detriment that he breaks it﴾ means: whoever breaks his covenant, the harm of his breaking returns only upon himself. It was also read with a kasra on the kaf (yankuthu).

﴿And whoever fulfills what he has covenanted with Allah﴾ is read with a damma on the ha' (alayhu), so that it is abqa after dropping the waw, as a means of emphasizing the lam of al-jalalah (the divine name Allah). It was also read with a kasra on it, meaning: and whoever fulfills his covenant.

﴿He will give him a great reward﴾ is Paradise. It was read as "bi-ma 'ahada" (with what He covenanted), and read as "fasanu'tihi" with the nun of majesty (nun al-'azama).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 48, verse 11:

﴿The ones who stayed behind from among the Bedouin will say to you﴾ They are the Bedouin of Ghifar, Muzaynah, Juhaynah, Ash'ja', Aslam and al-Dil, who stayed behind from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when he called upon the Bedouin and the people of the desert around Madinah to go out with him, at the time of his setting out for Makkah in the year of al-Hudaybiyah intending to perform 'umrah, fearing that the Quraysh might confront him with war or prevent him from the House. He, peace and blessings be upon him, put on the ihram and brought the sacrificial animals with him, so that it would be known that he did not intend war. But they were reluctant to go out, and said: "We would go to a people who attacked him in his own home in Madinah and killed his companions, so that we might fight them." Then Allah the Exalted revealed to him, peace and blessings be upon him, that they would make excuses and say ﴿Our wealth and our families kept us busy﴾, and that there was no one to take our place among them, to look after their affairs and protect them from being lost. It is also read "shaghghalat" with the doubled letter, for intensification.

﴿So ask forgiveness for us﴾ That Allah the Exalted may forgive us for staying behind from you, since that was not by choice but out of compulsion.

﴿They say with their tongues what is not in their hearts﴾ This is either a substitute for "will say," or a resumption serving to refute their claims in making excuse and asking forgiveness.

﴿Say﴾ as a reply to them when they offer you their false excuses.

﴿Who then has any power on your behalf against Allah?﴾ That is: who then, by Allah the Exalted's will and decree, can determine for your sake any benefit?

﴿If He intends harm for you﴾ That is: what harms you, such as the destruction and loss of family and wealth, so that you would stay behind from going out to preserve them and to ward off harm from them. It is also read "durran" with a dammah.

﴿Or if He intends benefit for you﴾ That is: and who has power over any harm if He intends for you what benefits you, such as preserving your wealth and families? Then what need is there to stay behind for the sake of guarding them? This is a demonstration of the truth and a refutation of them according to the apparent implication of their lying statement. The generalization of harm and benefit covers what is anticipated upon going out, such as killing, defeat, victory and spoils; this is refuted by the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Rather, Allah is ever Acquainted with what you do﴾, for it is a turning away from what they said and a clarification of its falsehood after clarifying its corruption on the assumption of its truth. That is: the matter is not as you say, but rather Allah has been Acquainted with all that you do, of the deeds among which is your staying behind and what is from its beginnings.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 48, verse 12:

"And His saying, ﴿Nay, you thought﴾ ... etc. is a substitute for ﴿Allah was﴾ ... etc., explaining the vagueness in it, i.e., "Nay, you thought."

﴿that the Messenger and the believers would never return to their families again﴾, by the mushriks utterly annihilating them. So you feared that if you were with them, what had befallen them would befall you, and therefore you stayed behind, not because of the false excuses you mentioned. Al-ahlun (the families) is the plural of ahl (family), and it may also be pluralized as ahalat, like aradat, by considering the feminine ta' (ta' al-ta'nith) in it. As for al-ahali, it is a collective noun (ism jam'), like al-layali. It has also been read as ﴿ila ahlihim﴾ (to their family, singular).

﴿And that was made attractive in your hearts﴾, and you accepted it and busied yourselves with your own concerns, paying no heed to them. It has also been read as "zayyana" (with the verb in the active voice), attributing it to Allah, glory be to Him, or to Satan.

﴿And you harboured an evil suspicion﴾. What is meant by it is either the first suspicion, with the repetition serving to intensify the reproach and to brand it as evil, or it is a broader category that includes it and other corrupt suspicions, among which is the suspicion that his prophethood (peace be upon him) is not valid, for one who firmly believes in its validity would not entertain in his thoughts the notion of annihilation that was mentioned.

﴿And you were a people deserving of destruction﴾. That is, ruined before Allah, deserving of His wrath and punishment, on the basis that it is the plural of ba'ir (like a'idh and 'uudh); or corrupt in your souls, hearts and intentions, with no good in you. It has been said that bur comes from bara (as halk comes from halak), in form and meaning, and for this reason it is used to describe the singular, the masculine plural and the feminine."

(p-108) ﴿And whoever does not believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ is a new statement from Him, exalted is He, not included in the speech that was taught; it confirms their ruin and explains its manner. That is: and whoever does not believe in both of them, like the condition of these who stayed behind.

﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the disbelievers a blazing Fire﴾ That is, for them. The phrase "the disbelievers" was placed in the position of the pronoun to indicate that whoever does not combine belief in Allah and His Messenger is a disbeliever, and that he deserves the Fire (sa'ir) because of his disbelief. The indefiniteness of "sa'iran" (a blazing Fire) is for magnification (tahwil), or because it is a particular kind of fire.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 48, verse 14:

﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, and whatever is in them; He disposes of all of it as He wills.

﴿He forgives whom He wills﴾ to forgive him.

﴿And He punishes whom He wills﴾ to punish him, without anyone having any influence over Him in anything of them, in existence or non-existence. In this there is a cutting off of their vain hopes of his (ﷺ) seeking forgiveness for them.

﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾, exceedingly so in forgiveness and mercy toward whom He wills; and He wills only for those whose forgiveness wisdom requires, from among those who believe in Him and His Messenger. As for those other than these from among the disbelievers, they are definitively excluded from that.

﴿The ones left behind will say﴾, that is, those mentioned. His saying, ﴿when you set out to take spoils, to take them﴾, is a temporal clause (ẓarf) modifying what precedes it, not a conditional (sharṭ) governing what follows. That is: they will say, when you set out for the spoils of Khaybar, ﴿to take them﴾, in accordance with what He promised you and singled you out with, as a compensation for what you missed of the spoils of Makkah.

﴿Let us follow you﴾ to Khaybar, and let us witness the fighting against its people with you.

﴿They want to change the word of Allah﴾ by sharing in the spoils that He reserved for the people of al-Hudaybiyah. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, returned from al-Hudaybiyah in Dhu al-Hijjah of the sixth year and remained in al-Madinah for the rest of that month and the beginning of al-Muharram of the seventh year. Then he campaigned against Khaybar with those who had witnessed al-Hudaybiyah, conquered it, and gained great wealth, and he reserved it for them, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, had commanded him. It is also read as "kalima Allah" (kalim Allah), which is the plural of kalimah (word). Whichever reading is adopted, the intended meaning is what was mentioned of His promise, exalted is He, that the spoils of Khaybar belong specifically to the people of al-Hudaybiyah, not His saying, ﴿You will never go out with me, ever﴾, for that was in the campaign of Tabuk.

﴿Say﴾ (this is) to despair them.

﴿You will never follow us﴾, that is, do not follow us. This is a negation carrying the meaning of a prohibition, for emphasis.

﴿Thus Allah said before﴾, that is, at the time of the return from al-Hudaybiyah.

﴿Then they will say﴾ to the believers, upon hearing this prohibition.

﴿Rather, you envy us﴾, that is, that prohibition is not the ruling of Allah; rather, you envy us for sharing with you in the spoils. It is also read "tahsidūnanā" with a kasrah on the sin (tahsidūnanā). His saying, ﴿Rather, they did not comprehend﴾, that is, they did not understand.

﴿except a little﴾, except a little understanding, which is their shrewdness in worldly affairs. This is a refutation of their false saying and a description of them with something greater than envy and more grievous than immoderate ignorance (p-109) and poor understanding in matters of religion.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 48, verse 16:

﴿Say to those who lagged behind among the Bedouin﴾ He repeated their mention with this designation, for the sake of intensifying their blame.

﴿You will be called to a people of mighty military strength﴾ They are Banu Hanifa, the people of Musaylima the Liar, or others among those who apostatized after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or the polytheists, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You will fight them, or they will submit﴾. That is, one of two things will be the case: either fighting forever or Islam alone, not otherwise, as the reading "aw yuslimu" (or they submit) makes clear. As for others besides them, their fighting ends with the jizya (poll-tax) just as it ends with Islam. In this there is evidence for the imamate of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, since this call did not fit anyone else, unless it is established that they were Thaqif and Hawazin, for that was in the era of prophethood. Thus the perpetual negation of following is restricted to what occurred at the Battle of Khaybar, as Muhyi al-Sunna said. It was also said: they are Persia and the Romans. The meaning of ﴿yuslimun﴾ is "they submit," for the Romans are Christians and Persia are Magians, from whom the jizya is accepted.

﴿If you obey, Allah will give you a good reward﴾ It is the spoils of war in this world and Paradise in the Hereafter.

﴿But if you turn away﴾ from the call.

﴿as you turned away before﴾ at al-Hudaybiyya.

﴿He will punish you with a painful punishment﴾ because of the multiplication of your sin.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 48, verse 17:

﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor is there blame upon the lame, nor is there blame upon the sick﴾: that is, in staying behind from the military campaign, because of the excuse and infirmity they have. For the obligation (taklif) revolves around capability (al-istita'ah). The negation of blame for each of these groups, which are enumerated, indicates further concern for their affair and an extension of the scope of the dispensation (al-rukhsah).

﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger﴾: in what has been mentioned of commands and prohibitions.

﴿He will admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾: and it is read "nudkhilhu" with the plural of majesty (nun al-'azamah).

﴿And whoever turns away﴾: that is, from obedience.

﴿He will punish him﴾: and it is read with the nun (nu'adhdhibhu).

﴿with a painful punishment﴾: whose extent cannot be measured.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 48, verse 18:

﴿Indeed, Allah was pleased with the believers﴾ They are the ones whose pledge of allegiance has been mentioned, and by this verse the Pledge of Good Pleasure (bay'at al-Ridwan) was named. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree﴾ is in the accusative case governed by "was pleased" (radiya). The use of the present tense (sighat al-mudari') is to bring its scene vividly before the mind, and "under the tree" (tahta al-shajarah) is either related to it or to an implied element that is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to its object. It is narrated that when he, peace and blessings be upon him, halted at al-Hudaybiyah, he sent Khirash ibn Umayyah al-Khuza'i as a messenger to the people of Makkah. They intended to harm him, but the Ahabish (a confederation of tribes allied with Quraysh) prevented him, so he returned. Then he sent 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, who informed them that he, peace and blessings be upon him, had not come for war, but had come only as a visitor to this House, to honor its sanctity. They showed him respect and said: "If you wish to circumambulate the House, then do so." He said: "I will not circumambulate before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ does." He remained with them, and it was rumored that they had killed him. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "We will not depart until we engage the people in battle," and he called the people to the pledge of allegiance, and they pledged to him under the tree, and it was a samurah tree (a kind of acacia). It is also said it was a sidrah (lote tree), that they would fight the Quraysh and not flee. It is also narrated: that they would pledge to die before him and not flee. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to them: "You today are the best of the people of the earth." They numbered one thousand five hundred and twenty-five. It is also said: one thousand four hundred, and it is said: one thousand three hundred. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and He knew what was in their hearts﴾ is conjoined to "they pledged allegiance to you" (yubayi'unaka), because, as you have understood, it has the meaning of "they pledged to you" (bayi'uka), not to "was pleased" (radiya). For His good pleasure with them is consequent upon His knowledge, may He be exalted, of what was in their hearts of sincerity and purity of intention at the time of their pledge to him, peace and blessings be upon him. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿so He sent down tranquility upon them﴾ is conjoined to "was pleased" (radiya), meaning: He sent down upon them calm, security and tranquility of the soul by strengthening their hearts. It is also said: by means of reconciliation (al-sulh).

﴿and rewarded them with a near victory﴾ It is the conquest of Khaybar, immediately after their return from al-Hudaybiyah, as its details have already passed. It is also read "wa-atahum" (and gave them).

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 48, verse 19:

﴿And many spoils that they will take﴾. That is, the spoils of Khaybar. The shift to the second person (khitab) in the reading of al-A'mash, Talhah and Nafi' is to honour them in a context of favour (imtinan).

﴿And Allah is ever Mighty﴾: dominant.

﴿Wise﴾: observing what wisdom requires in His rulings and decrees.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 48, verse 20:

﴿And Allah promised you much booty⦆ — it is what He will bestow upon the believers until the Day of Resurrection.

﴿You will take it⦆ — at its appointed times, each one of them.

﴿So He hastened this for you⦆ — that is, the spoils of Khaybar.

﴿And He withheld the hands of the people from you⦆ — that is, the hands of the people of Khaybar and their allies from the Banu Asad and Ghatafan, when they came to support them; so Allah cast terror into their hearts and they turned back. It is also said: the hands of the people of Makkah, through the truce.

﴿And that it might be a sign for the believers⦆ — a sign by which they would recognize the truthfulness of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in his promise to them, made upon his return from al-Hudaybiyah, of the booty mentioned, the conquest of Makkah, and entry into the Sacred Mosque. The lam (la, "in order that") is connected either to an elided element that comes later, meaning: "and that it might be a sign for them, [He] did what He did of hastening and withholding"; or to another elided purpose clause belonging to one of the two verbs, meaning: "He hastened this for you, or withheld the hands of the people, so that you might seize it, and that it might be..., etc." Thus the waw is parenthetical according to the first reading, and conjunctive according to the second.

﴿And guide you⦆ — by that sign.

﴿To a straight path⦆ — which is trust in the bounty of Allah, the Exalted, and reliance upon Him in everything you do and everything you leave undone.

**﴿And another [booty]﴾**: this is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon "this" (hādhihi), meaning: He hastened for you this booty and another booty.

**﴿which you were not able to obtain﴾**: this refers to the spoils of Hawazin in the battle of Hunayn. Describing them as beyond your ability was because of the rout that had occurred among them before that, in order to increase their desire for them. His saying, exalted is He: **﴿Allah has encompassed it﴾** is another description of "another," conveying the ease of obtaining it in relation to His power, exalted is He, after explaining how difficult it was to attain according to their own capability. That is: Allah has indeed had power over it, gained mastery over it, and made you prevail over it. It has also been said: He preserved it for you and kept it from others. Still, it has been said that "another" is in the accusative governed by a hidden verb that is explained by "Allah has encompassed it," meaning: and Allah has decreed another. There is no doubt that the information about Allah's decreeing it, after its inclusion in the category of the booty promised by His saying, exalted is He: **﴿Allah promised you much booty that you will take﴾**, adds no further benefit; the benefit lies only (p-111) in explaining its hastening.

**﴿And Allah is ever, over all things, Competent﴾**: because His power, exalted is He, is intrinsic and is not specific to one thing over another.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 48, verse 22:

﴿And if those who disbelieve had fought you, they would have turned their backs⁠ ⁠﴾ That is: the people of Makkah, and they did not make peace with you. It was also said: the allies of Khaybar.

﴿They would have turned their backs﴾ defeated.

﴿Then they would not find a protector﴾ who would guard them.

﴿Nor a helper﴾ who would support them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 48, verse 23:

﴿The way of Allah that has passed before﴾ i.e., Allah ordained the victory of His prophets as an ancient way (sunnah) concerning those nations that passed away.

﴿And you will not find any change in the way of Allah﴾ i.e., alteration.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 48, verse 24:

﴿And it is He who withheld their hands from you and your hands from them in the heart of Makkah﴾, i.e., the hands of the envoys (sufaar) of Makkah.

﴿in the heart of Makkah﴾, i.e., within it.

﴿after He had given you victory over them﴾. This is because 'Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl set out with five hundred men toward al-Hudaybiyah, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Khalid ibn al-Walid at the head of a force. He defeated them until he drove them into the walls of Makkah, then he returned. It was also said that this happened on the day of the Conquest (al-Fath), and Abu Hanifah cited it as evidence that Makkah was conquered by force ('anwatan) and not by treaty (sulhan).

﴿And Allah is All-Seer of what you do﴾, of their fighting and their defeat at first, and of their being withheld from you afterward, which was for the glorifying of His Sacred House. It is also read with the yaa' (ya'malun, "what they do").

﴿All-Seer﴾, so He will reward you for that, or He will reward them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 48, verse 25:

﴿They are the ones who disbelieved and barred you from the Sacred Mosque, and the sacrificial animals from reaching their place of sacrifice.﴾ Read in the accusative (naṣb), as a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on the object pronoun in "ṣaddūkum." It was also read in the genitive (jarr), as a conjunction on "al-Masjid," with an elided genitive construction (ḥadhf al-muḍāf), meaning "and [the barring of] the sacrifice of the offering." It was also read in the nominative (rafʿ), meaning "and the offering was barred." The phrase ﴿maʿkūfan﴾ ("detained") is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from "al-hady" (the offering), meaning "restrained." The phrase ﴿an yablugha maḥillahu﴾ ("from reaching its place of sacrifice") is either a substitution of part (badal ishtimāl) from "al-hady," or an accusative after the removal of the preposition (naz' al-khāfid), meaning "restrained from reaching its place, where its sacrifice is performed." Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, used this as evidence that the place of sacrifice for one who is prevented (al-muḥṣar) is the Haram. They said: "Part of al-Hudaybiyya is within the Haram." It is narrated that the tents of the Prophet ﷺ were in al-Hill (outside the Haram) while his place of prayer was in the Haram, and there his offerings were sacrificed, ﷺ. The intended meaning is that they were barred from their customary place of sacrifice, which is Mina.

﴿And had there not been believing men and believing women whom you did not know, [that] you might trample them, and thereby incur on their account a liability without knowledge.﴾ "Did not know" means you did not recognize them individually due to their mingling. This is an attributive clause (ṣifa) for "rijāl" and "nisāʾ." The phrase ﴿an taṭaʾūhum﴾ means "that you might strike them and destroy them," and is a substitution of part (badal ishtimāl) from "hum," or from the object pronoun in "taʿlamūhum."

﴿Then there would befall you from them﴾ meaning "from their side."

﴿a liability (maʿarrah)﴾ meaning hardship and something disliked, such as the obligation of blood-money or expiation for killing them, grief over them, reproach from the disbelievers, the evil of their speech, and sin through negligence in searching for them. It is a noun of place (mafʿalah) from ʿarrahu, when something he dislikes befalls and afflicts him.

﴿without knowledge﴾ is connected to "an taṭaʾūhum," meaning "not knowing about them." The answer to "law-lā" (had it not been for) is omitted, due to what the context indicates. The meaning: Had it not been for the aversion that you would destroy believing people among the disbelievers without knowing them, so that a disliked outcome would befall you on that account, He would have not restrained your hands from them. The phrase ﴿That Allah may admit into His mercy﴾ is connected to what the omitted answer indicates, as if it were said: "Rather, He restrained them from them, so that by that restraint, which leads to the conquest without a prohibited harm, He might admit into His vast mercy, in both its aspects."

﴿whom He wills﴾, namely the believers, for they were outside the worldly mercy, of which security is part, being oppressed under the hands of the disbelievers. As for the otherworldly mercy, they were not entirely deprived of it, yet they fell short in establishing the rites of worship as they should be. Therefore, enabling them to establish these in the most complete manner is an admission of them into the otherworldly mercy. It has been permitted that ﴿whom He wills﴾ refers to those among the polytheists who desired Islam, but the phrase ﴿if they had been separated﴾ ... etc. rejects this, for supposing separation and the consequent punishment upon it requires that the distinction between the two groups by faith and disbelief had already definitively been established before the separation, that is, "if they had separated and some of them had been distinguished from others." It was also read as "law tazāyalū."

﴿We would have punished those of them who disbelieved with a painful punishment﴾ through the killing of their fighters and the taking captive of their offspring. The sentence is a resumptive clause (mustaʾnafa) that confirms what precedes it.

﴿Idh ja'ala alladhina kafaru﴾ (when those who disbelieved made) is in the accusative, governed either by "udhkur" (remember) as a direct object (al-maf'uliyya), or by "'adhaban" (a punishment) as an adverb of time (al-zarfiyya). It has also been said that it is governed by an implied verb. May God show you kindness, whichever of these is the case. The placing of the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) in the position of their pronoun serves to censure them through what is in the relative clause (hayyiz al-sila), and to give the reason for the ruling by it. The verb "ja'ala" (made) may mean "to cast" (al-ilqa'), in which case His saying ﴿fi qulubihim al-hamiyya﴾ (in their hearts, zealotry), meaning arrogance and haughtiness, is connected to it. Or it may mean "to make" (al-taysir), in which case the phrase is connected to an implied word that is its second object, meaning: they made it firm and established in their hearts.

﴿hamiyyata al-jahiliyya﴾ (the zealotry of ignorance) is an apposition (badal) to "al-hamiyya", meaning: the zealotry of the ignorant creed, or the zealotry arising from ignorance. His saying ﴿fa-anzala Allahu sakinatahu 'ala rasulihi wa 'ala al-mu'minin﴾ (then God sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers) is, according to the first reading, coordinated (ma'tuf) with "ja'ala", and the purpose is to remind of the good conduct of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the believers, through God's granting of success, and of the bad conduct of the disbelievers. According to the second reading, it is understood from the conditional clause of impossibility (al-jumla al-imtina'iyya), as if it were said: they did not separate, so We did not punish them; then He sent down... and so on. According to the third reading, it is an explanation of the implied word. "Al-sakina" (tranquility) means steadfastness and dignity.

It is narrated that when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) alighted at al-Hudaybiya, Quraysh sent Suhayl ibn 'Amr al-Qurashi, Huwaytib ibn 'Abd al-'Uzza and Mukarraz ibn Hafs ibn al-Ahnaf, to propose to the Prophet (ﷺ) that he return that year, on condition that Quraysh would leave Mecca free for him for three days in the following year. He agreed to this, and they wrote a document between them. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: "Write: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful." They said: "We do not know what this is. Write: In Your name, O Allah." Then he said: "Write: This is what Muhammad, the Messenger of God, agreed upon with the people of Mecca." They said: "If we knew that you were the Messenger of God, we would not have barred you from the House, nor fought you. Write: This is what Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah agreed upon with the people of Mecca." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Write what they want." The believers resolved to refuse this and to attack them, so God sent down tranquility upon them, and they grew composed and forbearing.

﴿wa alzamahum kalimata al-taqwa﴾ (and He made them adhere to the word of piety) means the word of testimony (kalimat al-shahada), or "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful", or "Muhammad is the Messenger of God". It has also been said that "the word of piety" is the fulfilment of the covenant and steadfastness in it, and its attribution to piety is because it is the cause of piety and its foundation. Or it means the word of its people (kalimat ahliha).

﴿wa kanu ahaqqa biha﴾ (and they were more entitled to it), meaning characterised by greater entitlement to it, since the elative form (sighat al-tafdil) here denotes increase in general. It has also been said: more entitled to it than the disbelievers.

﴿wa ahlaha﴾ (and its people) means those who were fit for it (al-musta'hil laha).

﴿wa kana Allahu bikulli shay'in 'alima﴾ (and God is ever Knowing of all things): He knows the due right of everything, and so guides it to its deserving recipient.

﴿Allah has certainly made true to His Messenger the vision﴾. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw, before he set out for al-Hudaybiyya, that he and his companions had entered Mecca in safety, with their heads shaved and their hair cut short. He related the vision to his companions, and they rejoiced and were glad, and they supposed that they would enter it that same year. When that was delayed, ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy, ʿAbd Allah ibn Nufayl and Rifaʿa ibn al-Harith said: "By Allah, we did not shave or cut our hair, and we did not see the Sacred Mosque." Then it was revealed. That is, He confirmed him (ﷺ) in his vision, as in the saying of people, "The tooth of his camel told me the truth" (ṣadaqanī sinn bakrih). Its realization is that He showed him a true vision.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿in truth﴾, is either an adjectival qualifier (ṣifa) of an omitted emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar muʾakkad), meaning: a truth connected with the truth, that is, with a sound purpose and profound wisdom, which is the distinguishing of the one firm in faith from the one wavering in it. Or it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of "the vision", meaning: connected with the truth, not of the kind of confused dreams (aḍghāth al-aḥlām). It has also been permitted that it is an oath by "the Truth", which is one of the names of Allah Exalted, or by the opposite of falsehood.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿you will surely enter the Sacred Mosque﴾, is its answer (jawāb). According to the first two possibilities, it is the answer of an omitted oath, meaning: "By Allah, you will surely enter..." etc.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿if Allah wills﴾, is a conditioning of the promise by the will, in order to teach the servants; or it is to indicate that some of them will not enter it, through death, absence or other than that. Or it is a report of what the angel of the vision said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) first, when he said it to his companions, peace and blessings be upon him.

﴿Secure﴾ (āminīn) is a circumstantial clause from the subject of "you will enter". The conditional clause is parenthetical (iʿtirāḍ), and likewise His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿with your heads shaved and your hair cut short﴾, meaning: some of you shaving and others cutting short. It has been said that "shaving" (muḥallaqīn) is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "secure", so the clauses are interlocked (mutadākhila).

﴿Fear not﴾ is an emphatic circumstantial clause (ḥāl muʾakkida) from the subject of "you will enter", or of "secure", or of "shaving", or of "cutting short", or it is a resumptive clause (isti'nāf), meaning: "you will not fear after that."

﴿So He knew what you did not know﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to "has made true". What is meant by His knowledge, Exalted is He, is active knowledge (al-ʿilm al-fiʿlī), connected to an event occurring after what is conjoined to it. That is: so He knew, following what He showed him in the true vision, what you did not know of the wisdom that prompted the advance of what bears witness to the truth as active knowledge.

﴿Then He made﴾ means: for its sake.

﴿Besides that﴾ means: besides the realization of the fulfilment of what he saw, of entering the Sacred Mosque, etc.

﴿A near victory﴾, and it is the conquest of Khaybar. What is meant by His making it is His promise and its fulfilment without delay, so that it might be taken as evidence for the truth of the vision, as he said, "and that it might be a sign for the believers." As for taking "mā" in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿what you did not know﴾ to mean the wisdom behind delaying the conquest of Mecca until the following year, as the majority inclined to, it is rejected by the particle "fa" (then), for His knowledge of that is certainly prior to the showing of the vision.

﴿He is the One who sent His Messenger with guidance﴾, meaning accompanied by it, or because of it, and for its sake.

﴿and the religion of truth﴾, meaning and with the religion of Islam.

﴿that He may make it prevail over all religion﴾, meaning that He may exalt it over the whole category of religion, with all its individual forms, which are the differing religions. This is done by abrogating (naskh, the replacement of one ruling by another) those rulings that were true but were among the rulings that change with the changing of eras, and by manifesting the falsehood of what was false. Or it is done by empowering the Muslims over the people of all other religions, since there is no people of any religion except that the Muslims have subdued them. In this there is an emphasis on the promise of conquest, and a settling of the hearts of the believers, that He, glorified is He, will open for them cities and grant them such dominance over the regions that they can settle in them. This refers to the conquest of Mecca.

﴿And sufficient is Allah as a witness﴾, meaning as a witness that what He promised will certainly come to pass, or as a witness to the prophethood of His Prophet, upon him be peace and blessings, by manifesting miracles.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 48, verse 29:**

﴿Muhammad﴾ is the predicate (khabar) of a deleted subject (mubtada', subject). His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿the Messenger of God﴾, is either an apposition (badal), an explicative (bayan), or a descriptive (na't, adjective). The meaning is: "That is the Messenger sent with guidance and the religion of truth: Muhammad, the Messenger of God." It has also been said that ﴿Muhammad﴾ is the subject (mubtada') and "the Messenger of God" is its predicate (khabar), and the sentence explains what was witnessed to (al-mashhud bihi). His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿and those with him﴾, is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is ﴿are severe against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves﴾. ﴿Ashidda'* (severe)﴾ is the plural of shadid, and ﴿ruhama'* (merciful)﴾ is the plural of rahim. The meaning is that they show severity and firmness toward those who oppose their religion, and mercy and compassion toward those who share their religion, as in His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿humbled before the believers, mighty against the disbelievers﴾. It has been read as ﴿ashidda'a﴾ and ﴿ruhama'a﴾ in the accusative, either as a expression of praise (mad'h) or as a circumstantial state (hal) from the concealed pronoun in ma'ahu (with him), since it occurs as a relative clause (silah). In that case the predicate is His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿You see them bowing and prostrating﴾, meaning: you witness them in the state of bowing and prostrating, because of their constancy in the prayers. On the first reading, it is another predicate, or a resumptive sentence (isti'naf). His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿seeking bounty from God and approval﴾, meaning reward and good pleasure, is either another predicate, or a circumstantial state from the pronoun in ﴿you see them﴾, or from the concealed pronoun in ﴿bowing, prostrating﴾, or a resumptive sentence built on a question arising from the explanation of their constancy in bowing and prostration, as if it were said: "What do they want by that?" So it was answered: "They seek bounty from God..." etc.

﴿Their mark﴾ means their characteristic appearance (samt). It has been read as ﴿simya'uhum﴾ with a yā' after the mīm and a long vowel, and both are dialectal forms (lughatan). There is a third dialect, ﴿al-sima'*﴾ with a long vowel, which is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿in their faces﴾, meaning: on their foreheads. His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿from the trace of prostration﴾, is a circumstantial state (hal) from the concealed element in the prepositional phrase (al-jar), meaning: from the effect that the frequency of prostration leaves.

As for what has been transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ), in his statement, peace and blessings be upon him: ﴿Do not worship your forms﴾, meaning: do not make them into idols (lā tusammūhā), it applies only to the case where one presses his forehead onto the ground in order to produce that mark on it, and that is pure show (riya') and hypocrisy. The discussion here concerns the mark that appears on the forehead of the one who prostrates (al-sajjad), who does not prostrate except sincerely for the face of God, Mighty and Majestic. Imam Zayn al-'Abidin and 'Ali ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, were called "possessors of the calluses" (dhū al-thafanat), because the frequency of their prostrations produced, at the places of contact with them, marks resembling the calluses (thafanat) of a camel. One of their poets said:

*The abodes of 'Ali, Husayn and Ja'far,*
*and Hamza, and al-Sajjad, possessor of the calluses.*

It has also been said: the paleness of the face is from fear of God, Exalted is He. It has also been said: the moisture of ablution and the dust of the earth. It has also been said: the brightening of their faces from the length of their night prayers. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: ﴿Whoever's night prayer is abundant, his face becomes beautiful by day﴾. It has been read as ﴿min athar al-sujud﴾ and ﴿min ithr al-sujud﴾ with a kasra on the hamza.

﴿That﴾ refers to what was mentioned of their noble attributes (min nu'utihim al-jalilah). The demonstrative carries the sense of distance despite the nearness of the time of what is pointed to, to indicate the elevation of their rank and the remoteness of their station in excellence. It is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿their description﴾, meaning: their wondrous description, which in its strangeness functions as a proverb (al-amthal). His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿in the Torah﴾, is a circumstantial state from ﴿their description﴾, and the governing element (al-'amil) is the sense of the demonstrative. His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿and their description in the Gospel﴾, is conjoined ('atf) to the first ﴿their description﴾, as if it were said: "That is their description in the Torah and the Gospel." The repetition of ﴿their description﴾ is to emphasize its strangeness and to increase its establishment. His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿like a seed that sends out its shoot﴾ ... etc., is a resumed illustration (tamthil mustanaf), meaning: they are like a seed that sent forth its sprouts. It has also been said: it is an explanation of ﴿that﴾, on the basis that it is a vague demonstrative. It has also been said: it is a predicate for His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿and their description in the Gospel﴾, on the basis that the sentence was complete at His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿their description in the Torah﴾. It has been read as ﴿shatha'hu﴾ with two fathas; ﴿shatahu﴾ with a fatha on the ta' and a lightened hamza; ﴿shata'ahu﴾ with a long vowel; ﴿shatahu﴾ with the hamza dropped and its vowel transferred to the preceding letter; and ﴿shattuhu﴾ with the hamza changed into a waw.

﴿So he strengthened it﴾ means he made it strong, from al-mu'azarah (assistance), in the sense of mu'awanah (help), or from al-izar, which is aid. It has been read as ﴿fa'azarahu﴾ with lightening, and ﴿azzarahu﴾ with doubling, meaning: he strengthened its support (shadda azrahu). His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿so it grew thick﴾, means it became thick after it had been thin.

﴿So it stood firm upon its stalk﴾ means it stood straight upon its stem, the plural of sāq (stalk). It has been read as ﴿su'uqihi﴾ with a hamza.

﴿It pleases the sowers﴾, by its strength, its density, its thickness and the beauty of its appearance. This is a parable God, Mighty and Majestic, made for His companions, peace and blessings be upon him, who were few at the beginning of Islam, then they increased and became firmly established, so their affair ascended day by day until it pleased people. It has also been said: it is written in the Gospel: "A people will come forth who sprout like the growth of a seed; they will command the good and forbid the evil." His statement, Exalted is He, ﴿so that He may enrage the disbelievers by them﴾, is a reason (ʿillah) for what the speech implies of their resemblance to the seed in its growth and establishment, or for what follows it, His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿God has promised those among them who believe and do righteous deeds forgiveness and a great reward﴾. For when the disbelievers hear of what has been prepared for the believers in the Hereafter, along with the honor they have in this world, that enrages them with the most intense rage. The particle ﴿min﴾ (among) is explicative (lil-bayan). It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ): «Whoever recites Surah al-Fath, it is as if he had been among those who witnessed with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) the conquest of Mecca.»
